newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech govt faces pressure as economic woes grow.
newsitem.headline: Czech govt faces pressure as economic woes grow.

text.p: Tension is growing within the Czech Republic's ruling coalition and some analysts say the government, criticised for its handling of a sharp economic downturn, may not last until the end of the year.

Criticism has been mounting and dissent between coalition partners has grown since Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's three-party centre-right government last month unveiled measures designed to kick-start the economy.
"The coalition is more fragile than at any time in the past," said political analyst Jiri Pehe of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty. "I think they will not survive the end of the year."
He said the economic package, rather than signalling unity, had highlighted differences between partners.

With parliamentary elections due in June 2000, an opinion poll released on Wednesday -- the first since the measures were announced -- showed Klaus's government was at its lowest support rating since last June's elections.

The survey, conducted by the state-run Institute for Public Opinion Research in early May, put the coalition's support at 42.5 percent, down 1.5 percentage points from April and four points lower than in January.
After several years of consumption-led growth, the Czech economy has slowed recently with output declining severely.
Klaus, the architect of the country's economic transformation, admitted last month it would be a success if the economy, after real growth of 4.4 percent in 1996, grew 2.7 percent this year.
The country's image has also been tarnished by several financial scandals, including alleged asset-stripping at investment funds holding many Czechs' savings.
President Vaclav Havel, in a weekly radio address on Sunday, expressed concern at the political and economic situation, and this week began talks with the coalition leaders.

"When there is talk that the political atmosphere in the country is not very good, when the government is being criticised ... then I ask myself if there is a lack of programme in the sense of a long-term vision," Havel said.
Long-serving Industry and Trade Minister Vladimir Dlouhy, frequently criticised for the state of the economy, said at the weekend he was considering stepping down at the end of the year.

The government, dominated by Klaus's Civic Democratic Party (ODS) and including the conservative Civic Democratic Alliance (ODA) and the centrist Christian Democrats (KDU-CSL) has been in power since 1992, pre-dating the 1993 split of Czechoslovakia.
Some analysts say the coalition has run out of steam now that things have become more difficult.

"The mistake is that for a long time some government representatives have been covering up the reality, fogging and lying," said Rudolf Kucera, political scientist at Prague's Charles University's social sciences faculty.
He said new elections would be the worst possible outcome but added: "At least there has to be a thorough restructuring of the cabinet by the end of the year".
ODA leader Michael Zantovsky, a former Washington ambassador, said this could not happen overnight. "It will need several weeks or a few months," he told Czech radio.
After the kick-start package, which included public spending cuts and strict targets for wage growth, was announced, many analysts expected senior ministers to go.
Deputy finance minister Vladimir Rudlovcak quit before the package and KDU-CSL Local Development Minister Jaromir Schneider quit afterwards.

"I do not see the situation as ready for the fall of the government as a whole," said Kucera. "But I see the resignation of Vaclav Klaus as a necessary step...also the finance minister and trade minister."
But Patria Finance economist Vladimir Kreidl does not see the government falling, saying it had acknowledged the economy's problems and come up with ideas to address them.
"I think this coalition will survive until the next Senate (upper house) elections in fall 1998," he said.
